To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified a subset of direct GATA- 1 target genes and have gained insights into GATA1-mediated gene activation or repression in vivo.

the transcription factor GATA1 is required for erythroid differentiation and functions as an activating or repressive transcription factor, depending on gene context, and that GATA1 occupancy is a better predictor of gene activation or repression than GATA1 binding site number or motif sequence.

the GATA-1 transcription factor regulates gene expression by binding to specific genomic sites, and that the presence of other transcription factors, such as Zbtb7A and PRC2, is involved in the activation and repression of GATA- 1-regulated genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transcription factor GATA1 and the regulation of gene expression in the developing erythrocyte.
the transcription factor GATA1 and its role in the development of the blood system.
the transcription factor GATA1 and its ability to control the gene expression programs that lead to red blood cell production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

GATA-1 binds a wide range of genes in vivo, but only a subset of these genes are directly regulated by GATA-1, which is further dependent on the presence of SLC/TAL1, Zbtb7, and PRC2, as well as the presence or absence of GATA-2.
the binding of GATA1 to a gene is not enough to predict whether it will be activated or repressed.
GATA-1 occupancy is not the only factor that determines the transcriptional outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

GATA-1 occupancy is associated with gene activation and repression, but the presence of Scl/Tal1 and Zbtb7 (LRF) can distinguish activation from repression, and the occupancy of PRC2 is associated with GATA-1 mediated gene repression.
the GATA-1 transcription factor is a critical regulator of gene expression in the erythroid lineage and that the GATA motif is a critical determinant of GATA-activity.

the GATA-1 transcription factor has the ability to distinguish between gene activation and gene repression in vivo, and that this is mediated by the presence or absence of other transcription factors and chromatin modifiers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GATA-1 binding alone does not determine gene activation versus repression.
the GATA-1 genome-wide binding landscape is more complicated than previously anticipated.
GATA-1 occupancy alone does not predict gene activation versus repression.
